A secret revelation was made to Moses while in the presence of Pharaoh, that he might give warning of the last dreadful judgment, before he went out. Their masters, who had abused them in their work, would have sent them away empty; but God provided that the labourers should not lose their hire, and ordered them to demand it now, at their departure, and it was given to them. God will right the injured, who in humble silence commit their cause to him; and none are losers at last by patient suffering. The Lord gave them favour in the sight of the Egyptians, by making it appear how much he favoured them. He also changed the spirit of the Egyptians toward them, and made them to be pitied of their oppressors. Those that honour God, he will honour.
[Exod.11.4-Exod.11.10]
Verses 4-10
The death of all the first-born in Egypt at once: this plague had been the first threatened, but is last executed. See how slow God is to wrath. The plague is foretold, the time is fixed; all their first-born should sleep the sleep of death, not silently, but so as to rouse the families at midnight. The prince was not too high to be reached by it, nor the slaves at the mill too low to be noticed. While angels slew the Egyptians, not so much as a dog should bark at any of the children of Israel. It is an earnest of the difference there shall be in the great day, between God's people and his enemies. Did men know what a difference God puts, and will put to eternity, between those that serve him and those that serve him not, religion would not seem to them an indifferent thing; nor would they act in it with so much carelessness as they do. Pharaoh was hardened, yet he was compelled to abate his stern and haughty demands, till the Israelites got full freedom. The Passover is instituted (verses 1–20)

The Lord makes everything new for people whom he releases from Satan's slavery and brings into his family.

The time of their deliverance becomes the beginning of a new life.

God instructed every Israelite household to kill a lamb on the night they would leave Egypt.

Where a family was small, two or three families could share one lamb.

They were to eat it in the manner God prescribed and put some of its blood on their doorposts.

This would distinguish their homes from Egyptian homes.

When the Lord's angel killed the firstborn of Egypt, he would pass over every house marked with the lamb's blood.

This is where the name of the holy feast comes from.

Israel was to celebrate the Passover every year, remembering its preservation and deliverance from Egypt and recognizing in it a striking picture of Christ.

The people's safety was not a reward for their righteousness.

It was a gift of mercy.

Through this ordinance they learned that God's blessings came to them through the shedding and application of blood.

First, the Passover lamb pointed to Christ.

Christ is our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

He is the Lamb of God (John 1:29), and the book of Revelation often calls him the Lamb.

The animal was to be in the prime of life.

Christ gave himself in the midst of his days, not as an infant at Bethlehem.

The lamb had to be without blemish.

Jesus likewise had no fault; even the judge who condemned him declared him innocent.

The lamb was chosen four days beforehand.

This pictured the appointment of Christ as Savior, both in God's purpose and in his promise.

The lamb was killed and roasted over fire.

This pictured Christ's painful suffering and death, even death on the cross.

God's wrath is like fire, and Christ became a curse for us.

Not one of the lamb's bones was to be broken.

This was fulfilled in Christ (John 19:33) and pointed to his unbroken strength.

Second, the sprinkled blood pointed to the application of Christ's death.

The lamb's blood had to be put on the doors.

This pictured the personal application of the benefits of Christ's death.

We must receive the atonement (Romans 5:11).

Faith is like the bunch of hyssop with which the blood is applied.

Through faith we receive for ourselves God's promises and the benefits of Christ's blood contained in them.

The blood was placed openly on the doorposts.

This pointed to our public profession of faith in Christ.

It was not placed on the threshold.

This warns us never to trample underfoot the blood of the covenant.

It is precious blood, and it must be precious to us.

The blood on the doors protected Israel from the destroying angel, who had no authority in the houses where it was found.

In the same way, Christ's blood protects believers from God's wrath, the curse of the law, and eternal condemnation (Romans 8:1).

Third, eating the lamb pictured our duty to receive Christ by faith.

The lamb was not merely to be looked at.

It had to be eaten.

So we must receive Christ as our own by faith and draw spiritual strength and nourishment from him, as we draw nourishment from food (John 6:53, 55).

The whole lamb had to be eaten.

Those who feed on Christ by faith must receive the whole Christ.

They must accept not only his crown but also his yoke and his cross.

The lamb had to be eaten that night, not saved until morning.

Christ is offered to us today, and we must receive him while it is still called today, before the sleep of death overtakes us.

Bitter herbs accompanied the meal, recalling the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.

We must receive Christ with grief and brokenness of heart as we remember our sin.

Christ will be sweet to us when sin has become bitter.

The Israelites ate standing, with their staffs in hand, ready to depart.

When we feed on Christ through faith, we must leave sin's rule behind and loosen our attachment to the world and everything in it.

We must give up everything for him, knowing that this is no loss (Hebrews 13:13–14).

Fourth, the feast of unleavened bread pictured the Christian life (1 Corinthians 5:7–8).

Once we have received Jesus Christ as Lord, we should continue finding our joy in him.

No work was to interrupt the feast.

In the spiritual application, we should allow no worldly anxiety that is incompatible with this holy joy or diminishes it.

The Jews took great care that no leaven remained in their houses.

Our celebration must likewise be free of malice and full of love, free of hypocrisy and full of sincerity.

The feast was established as a lasting ordinance.

Throughout our lives, we must keep feeding on Christ, rejoicing in him, and gratefully remembering the great things he has done for us.

Israel is instructed to observe the Passover (verses 21–28)

On the night Egypt's firstborn were to die, no Israelite was to leave the house until the time came to depart from Egypt.

Their safety rested in the blood that had been applied.

To move outside its protection would put them in danger.

They were to remain inside and wait for the Lord's salvation.

That is a good thing for us to do as well.

In later generations, parents were to teach their children carefully what this ceremony meant.

It is good for children to ask questions about God.

Those who ask about the right way will find it.

The annual celebration looked in two directions.

First, backward, so that the people would remember what God had done for them and their ancestors.

Past mercies shown to us or to earlier generations must never be forgotten.

Remembering them brings praise to God and strengthens faith.

Second, forward, as a pledge of the great sacrifice the Lamb of God would make when the time was fulfilled.

Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us.

His death is our life.

Egypt's firstborn die, and Israel is released (verses 29–36)

For three days and nights the Egyptians had lived in terror because of the darkness.

Now their rest was broken by a much more dreadful disaster.

The firstborn—the joy and hope of their families—were struck down.

The Egyptians had killed Hebrew children.

Now God struck their children.

The judgment reached from Pharaoh's throne to the dungeon.

Princes and ordinary laborers are equal before God's judgments.

The destroying angel entered every dwelling not marked with blood.

Not one such house escaped death.

Imagine the great cry that filled Egypt, the long, agonizing wailing from family after family.

Something similar will happen when the Son of Man comes to judge sinners for the last time.

God's sons, his firstborn people, were now set free.

People would do well to accept God's terms from the beginning, because he will never submit to theirs.

Pharaoh's pride was brought low, and he yielded.

God's word will stand.

Argument and delay accomplish nothing against it.

In their terror the Egyptians were willing to give generously to secure Israel's favor and make the people leave quickly.

In this way God ensured that Israel was paid for its hard labor and provided with what it needed for the journey.

Israel sets out for Succoth (verses 37–42)

The Israelites departed without delay.

A mixed multitude went with them.

Some may have wanted to escape a country devastated by plagues.

Others may have followed from curiosity, and perhaps a few because they loved Israel and its faith.

But among the Israelites there had always been some who were not truly Israelites.

There are still hypocrites in the church.

Henry dates this great event to 430 years after the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:17).

For all that time, the promised settlement had not yet come.

God's promises may not be fulfilled quickly, but they will be fulfilled at the proper time.

That night belonged to the Lord.

Its remarkable events were to be commemorated through every generation.

The great things God does for his people are not meant to be talked about for a few days and then forgotten.

They should be remembered through the ages—especially Christ's work of redemption.

Israel's first Passover night was indeed a night to remember.

But the last Passover night, when Christ was betrayed and the original Passover along with the other Jewish ceremonies came to an end, is still more worthy of remembrance.

Then a yoke heavier than Egypt's was broken from our necks.

A land better than Canaan was placed before us.

That redemption will be celebrated in heaven forever.

Who may share in the Passover (verses 43–51)

In later times, all the congregation of Israel was required to keep the Passover.

Everyone who shares in God's mercies should join in giving thanks and praise.

The New Testament Passover, the Lord's Supper, should not be neglected.

Foreigners who received circumcision could take part in Israel's Passover.

This was an early indication of God's favor toward the Gentiles.

It taught Israel that membership among a people favored by God, not simply physical descent from Abraham, gave someone access to the people's privileges.

Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).

His blood is the only ransom for our souls.

Without the shedding of his blood, there is no forgiveness of sins.

Without its application to us, there is no salvation.

Have we, through faith in Christ, placed ourselves under the protection of his atoning blood and found shelter from the judgment we deserve?

Do we remain near him, continually depending on him?

Do we profess our faith in the Redeemer and our debt to him so openly that everyone who sees us can tell to whom we belong?

Are we ready to serve him, walk in his ways, and separate ourselves from his enemies?

These questions matter enormously for our souls.

May the Lord guide our consciences to answer them truthfully.

Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
The beginning of the year changed, The passover instituted. | (1-20) |
The people instructed how to observe the passover. | (21-28) |

Verses 1-20
The Lord makes all things new to those whom he delivers from the bondage of Satan, and takes to himself to be his people. The time when he does this is to them the beginning of a new life. God appointed that, on the night wherein they were to go out of Egypt, each family should kill a lamb, or that two or three families, if small, should kill one lamb. This lamb was to be eaten in the manner here directed, and the blood to be sprinkled on the door-posts, to mark the houses of the Israelites from those of the Egyptians. The angel of the Lord, when destroying the first-born of the Egyptians, would pass over the houses marked by the blood of the lamb: hence the name of this holy feast or ordinance. The passover was to be kept every year, both as a remembrance of Israel's preservation and deliverance out of Egypt, and as a remarkable type of Christ. Their safety and deliverance were not a reward of their own righteousness, but the gift of mercy. Of this they were reminded, and by this ordinance they were taught, that all blessings came to them through the shedding and sprinkling of blood. Observe, 1. The paschal lamb was typical. Christ is our passover, [1Cor.5.7] 1Co 5:7. Christ is the Lamb of God, [John.1.29] Joh 1:29; often in the Revelation he is called the Lamb. It was to be in its prime; Christ offered up himself in the midst of his days, not when a babe at Bethlehem. It was to be without blemish; the Lord Jesus was a Lamb without spot: the judge who condemned Christ declared him innocent. It was to be set apart four days before, denoting the marking out of the Lord Jesus to be a Saviour, both in the purpose and in the promise. It was to be slain, and roasted with fire, denoting the painful sufferings of the Lord Jesus, even unto death, the death of the cross. The wrath of God is as fire, and Christ was made a curse for us. Not a bone of it must be broken, which was fulfilled in Christ, [John.19.33] Joh 19:33, denoting the unbroken strength of the Lord Jesus. 2. The sprinkling of the blood was typical. The blood of the lamb must be sprinkled, denoting the applying of the merits of Christ's death to our souls; we must receive the atonement, [Rom.5.11] Ro 5:11. Faith is the bunch of hyssop, by which we apply the promises, and the benefits of the blood of Christ laid up in them, to ourselves. It was to be sprinkled on the door-posts, denoting the open profession we are to make of faith in Christ. It was not to be sprinkled upon the threshold; which cautions us to take heed of trampling under foot the blood of the covenant. It is precious blood, and must be precious to us. The blood, thus sprinkled, was a means of preserving the Israelites from the destroying angel, who had nothing to do where the blood was. The blood of Christ is the believer's protection from the wrath of God, the curse of the law, and the damnation of hell, [Rom.8.1] Ro 8:1. [Rom.8.3] 3. The solemn eating of the lamb was typical of our gospel duty to Christ. The paschal lamb was not to be looked upon only, but to be fed upon. So we must by faith make Christ our own; and we must receive spiritual strength and nourishment from him, as from our food, see [John.6.53] Joh 6:53, [John.6.55] 55. It was all to be eaten; those who by faith feed upon Christ, must feed upon a whole Christ; they must take Christ and his yoke, Christ and his cross, as well as Christ and his crown. It was to be eaten at once, not put by till morning. To-day Christ is offered, and is to be accepted while it is called to-day, before we sleep the sleep of death. It was to be eaten with bitter herbs, in remembrance of the bitterness of their bondage in Egypt; we must feed upon Christ with sorrow and brokenness of heart, in remembrance of sin. Christ will be sweet to us, if sin be bitter. It was to be eaten standing, with their staves in their hands, as being ready to depart. When we feed upon Christ by faith, we must forsake the rule and the dominion of sin; sit loose to the world, and every thing in it; forsake all for Christ, and reckon it no bad bargain, [Heb.13.13] He 13:13, [Heb.13.14] 14. [Heb.13.4] 4. The feast of unleavened bread was typical of the Christian life, [1Cor.5.7] 1Co 5:7, [1Cor.5.8] 8. Having received Christ Jesus the Lord, we must continually delight ourselves in Christ Jesus. No manner of work must be done, that is, no care admitted and indulged, which does not agree with, or would lessen this holy joy. The Jews were very strict as to the passover, so that no leaven should be found in their houses. It must be a feast kept in charity, without the leaven of malice; and in sincerity, without the leaven of hypocrisy. It was by an ordinance for ever; so long as we live we must continue feeding upon Christ, rejoicing in him always, with thankful mention of the great things he has done for us.
[Exod.12.21-Exod.12.28]
Verses 21-28
That night, when the first-born were to be destroyed, no Israelite must stir out of doors till called to march out of Egypt. Their safety was owing to the blood of sprinkling. If they put themselves from under the protection of that, it was at their peril. They must stay within, to wait for the salvation of the Lord; it is good to do so. In after-times they should carefully teach their children the meaning of this service. It is good for children to ask about the things of God; they that ask for the way will find it. The keeping of this solemnity every year was, 1. To look backward, that they might remember what great things God had done for them and their fathers. Old mercies, to ourselves, or to our fathers, must not be forgotten, that God may be praised, and our faith in him encouraged. 2. It was designed to look forward, as an earnest of the great sacrifice of the Lamb of God in the fulness of time. Christ our passover was sacrificed for us; his death was our life.
[Exod.12.29-Exod.12.36]
Verses 29-36
The Egyptians had been for three days and nights kept in anxiety and horror by the darkness; now their rest is broken by a far more terrible calamity. The plague struck their first-born, the joy and hope of their families. They had slain the Hebrews' children, now God slew theirs. It reached from the throne to the dungeon: prince and peasant stand upon the same level before God's judgments. The destroying angel entered every dwelling unmarked with blood, as the messenger of woe. He did his dreadful errand, leaving not a house in which there was not one dead. Imagine then the cry that rang through the land of Egypt, the long, loud shriek of agony that burst from every dwelling. It will be thus in that dreadful hour when the Son of man shall visit sinners with the last judgment. God's sons, his first-born, were now released. Men had better come to God's terms at first, for he will never come to theirs. Now Pharaoh's pride is abased, and he yields. God's word will stand; we get nothing by disputing, or delaying to submit. In this terror the Egyptians would purchase the favour and the speedy departure of Israel. Thus the Lord took care that their hard-earned wages should be paid, and the people provided for their journey.
[Exod.12.37-Exod.12.42]
Verses 37-42
The children of Israel set forward without delay. A mixed multitude went with them. Some, perhaps, willing to leave their country, laid waste by plagues; others, out of curiosity; perhaps a few out of love to them and their religion. But there were always those among the Israelites who were not Israelites. Thus there are still hypocrites in the church. This great event was 430 years from the promise made to Abraham: see [Gal.3.17] Ga 3:17. So long the promise of a settlement was unfulfilled. But though God's promises are not performed quickly, they will be, in their season. This is that night of the Lord, that remarkable night, to be celebrated in all generations. The great things God does for his people, are to be not only a few days' wonder, but to be remembered throughout all ages; especially the work of our redemption by Christ. This first passover-night was a night of the Lord, much to be observed; but the last passover-night, in which Christ was betrayed and in which the first passover, with the rest of the Jewish ceremonies, was done away, was a night of the Lord, much more to be observed. Then a yoke, heavier than that of Egypt, was broken from off our necks, and a land, better than that of Canaan, set before us. It was a redemption to be celebrated in heaven, for ever and ever.
[Exod.12.43-Exod.12.51]
Verses 43-51
In times to come, all the congregation of Israel must keep the passover. All that share in God's mercies should join in thankful praises for them. The New Testament passover, the Lord's supper, ought not to be neglected by any. Strangers, if circumcised, might eat of the passover. Here is an early indication of favour to the gentiles. This taught the Jews that their being a nation favoured by God, entitled them to their privileges, not their descent from Abraham. Christ our passover is sacrificed for us, [1Cor.5.7] 1Co 5:7; his blood is the only ransom for our souls; without the shedding of it there is no remission; without the sprinkling of it there can be no salvation. Have we, by faith in him, sheltered our souls from deserved vengeance under the protection of his atoning blood? Do we keep close to him, constantly depending upon him? Do we so profess our faith in the Redeemer, and our obligations to him, that all who pass by may know to whom we belong? Do we stand prepared for his service, ready to walk in his ways, and to separate ourselves from his enemies? These are questions of vast importance to the soul; may the Lord direct our consciences honestly to answer them.

The firstborn are dedicated to God; the deliverance is remembered (verses 1–10)

God commanded Israel to dedicate its firstborn sons to him. This memorial joined two great events: the deaths of Egypt's firstborn, both human and animal, and Israel's deliverance from slavery.

The people were to remember that their lives had been spared through a ransom. That ransom pointed ahead to the atonement that would be made for sin at the appointed time.

Lives rescued from death are to be devoted to God's service.

Parents were not to think of their firstborn as belonging to them without first presenting them solemnly to God and acknowledging his claim upon them.

Whatever God spares for us through special mercy should be used for his honor. At the very least, we should acknowledge his goodness through grateful acts of devotion and charity.

Israel was to remember its departure from Egypt every year.

We should also remember the day of Christ's resurrection. In him we were raised from death's house of slavery.

Scripture does not expressly tell us the day of the year on which Christ rose, but it does tell us the day of the week. Henry therefore urges us to commemorate this greater deliverance weekly.

Israel observed the feast of unleavened bread. Under the gospel, we must do more than remember Christ in thought: we must also observe his holy Supper, as he commanded, in remembrance of him.

Parents must teach their children to know God. This is an ancient command to instruct them in the faith.

It is especially valuable to acquaint children with Bible history while they are young.

People who have God's law in their hearts should also have it on their lips. Speaking about it often strengthens their own hearts and teaches others.

The firstborn animals and the ransom (verses 11–16)

Firstborn animals that could not be offered as sacrifices had to be exchanged for animals that could, or else be destroyed.

Our own souls have been forfeited under God's justice. Unless Christ's sacrifice ransoms them, they will certainly perish.

These ordinances constantly reminded Israel of its duty to love and serve the Lord.

In a similar way, baptism and the Lord's Supper remind Christians of their profession and their duties—when these ordinances are explained and observed properly. They also give us opportunities to remind one another.

Israel takes the longer road (verses 17–20)

There were two possible routes from Egypt to Canaan.

One would take only a few days. The other, through the wilderness, was much longer.

God chose the longer route for his people.

The Egyptians would be drowned in the Red Sea, while the Israelites would be humbled and tested in the wilderness.

God's way is the right way, even when it seems a roundabout way.

If he does not lead us along the shortest path, we can be sure he leads us along the best one. We will see that clearly when we reach our journey's end.

The Philistines were formidable enemies. The Israelites needed to be prepared for the wars of Canaan through the hardships of the wilderness.

God measures his people's trials according to their strength (1 Corinthians 10:13).

The people departed in orderly formation. Henry records differing explanations of the formation: five abreast or divided into five companies.

They also carried Joseph's bones. This testified to their faith and hope that God would bring them to Canaan.

The Lord guides his people by cloud and fire (verses 21–22)

The Lord went ahead of Israel in a pillar—a visible sign of the divine presence.

Christ was with his church in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:9).

When God leads his people into a wilderness, he does not abandon or lose them there. He cares for them and leads them through it.

For Moses and the faithful Israelites, being sure of divine guidance was a great comfort.

We too may be sure that the Lord goes before us when we make his glory our goal, his word our rule, his Spirit the guide of our desires, and his providence the guide of our circumstances.

We cannot see him with our eyes. Now we must live by faith.

As Israel moved, the pillar went ahead and indicated the place where divine wisdom intended them to camp.

It sheltered them from the heat by day and gave them light at night.

God's word is likewise a lamp for our feet and a light for our path. Our Savior's love has provided it for us, and it testifies about Christ.

The Bible is to us what the pillar was to Israel.

Listen to the One who says that he is the light of the world: whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life (John 8:12).

Jesus Christ alone is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

He is made known to us in Scripture, and the Holy Spirit directs our souls to him in answer to prayer.

Verses 1-10
In remembrance of the destruction of the first-born of Egypt, both of man and of beast, and the deliverance of the Israelites out of bondage, the first-born males of the Israelites were set apart to the Lord. By this was set before them, that their lives were preserved through the ransom of the atonement, which in due time was to be made for sin. They were also to consider their lives, thus ransomed from death, as now to be consecrated to the service of God. The parents were not to look upon themselves as having any right in their first-born, till they solemnly presented them to God, and allowed his title to them. That which is, by special mercy, spared to us, should be applied to God's honour; at least, some grateful acknowledgment, in works of piety and charity, should be made. The remembrance of their coming out of Egypt must be kept up every year. The day of Christ's resurrection is to be remembered, for in it we were raised up with Christ out of death's house of bondage. The Scripture tells us not expressly what day of the year Christ rose, but it states particularly what day of the week it was; as the more valuable deliverance, it should be remembered weekly. The Israelites must keep the feast of unleavened bread. Under the gospel, we must not only remember Christ, but observe his holy supper. Do this in remembrance of him. Also care must be taken to teach children the knowledge of God. Here is an old law for catechising. It is of great use to acquaint children betimes with the histories of the Bible. And those who have God's law in their heart should have it in their mouth, and often speak of it, to affect themselves, and to teach others.

Israel complains; God promises bread from heaven (verses 1–12)

By the middle of the second month, the provisions Israel had brought from Egypt were gone. The people began to complain.

It is nothing new for people to describe the greatest kindness they have received as though it were the greatest injury.

They valued their deliverance so little that they wished they had died in Egypt—by the Lord's hand, meaning by the plagues that killed the Egyptians.

We cannot suppose that they had lived in plenty in Egypt. Nor did they need to fear starvation in the wilderness while they still possessed flocks and herds.

No one reasons more absurdly than people who are determined to complain.

When we begin to fret, we should remember that God hears every complaint we make.

Yet the Lord promised them a prompt and continuing supply of food.

He tested whether they would trust him, content to receive enough bread for each day as it came.

He was also testing whether they would serve him, and their ingratitude became plain.

When God struck Egypt with plagues, he showed that he was its Lord.

When he provided food for Israel, he showed that he was their God.

Quail and manna are provided (verses 13–21)

Quail came in the evening. The people were able to catch as many as they needed without difficulty.

Manna came down with the dew.

The Israelites called it manna, or manhu: “What is this?”

They could say of it, “This is the portion God has assigned us. We will receive it thankfully.”

It was pleasant and wholesome food.

It came from heaven. After the dew evaporated, the people saw small round pieces, like frost, resembling coriander seed and having the color of pearls.

Manna fell on six days of the week, with a double amount on the sixth.

If it was kept beyond one day, it developed worms and became foul—except when kept for the Sabbath.

The Israelites had never seen anything like it before.

They could grind it in a mill, crush it in a mortar, make it into cakes and bake it.

It continued for all forty years of their wilderness journey and wherever they camped, ceasing when they reached Canaan.

These features show that manna was different from anything familiar in their own day or ours.

They had to gather it every morning.

First, this teaches diligence and prudence.

We should provide food for ourselves and our families through honest, peaceful work, not through idleness or deceit.

God's generosity does not remove our responsibility to act.

Even when bread literally rained from heaven, the people had to gather it before they could eat it.

Second, this teaches contentment.

We should be satisfied with enough.

Those with the most possessions still need only food and clothing for themselves. Those with fewer possessions can generally enjoy these as well.

Thus, in actual enjoyment of life's necessities, the difference between rich and poor is not as great as the difference between what they possess.

The person who gathers much has nothing left over, and the one who gathers little does not lack what is needed.

Third, this teaches dependence on Providence.

They could go to sleep peacefully even with no bread anywhere in the camp.

They could trust God to provide their daily bread the next morning.

Their food was safer and more certain in God's storehouse than in their own tents—and would arrive fresher and sweeter.

See the folly of hoarding out of distrust.

People who thought themselves wiser than their neighbors saved manna for the next day in case God failed to provide it.

But their stored manna bred worms and became useless.

What is selfishly and fearfully hoarded may become the very thing most thoroughly wasted.

Such riches become corrupted (James 5:2–3).

The same wisdom, power and goodness that supplied food from heaven each day to Israel continues to bring food from the ground each year through the ordinary course of nature.

He gives us richly everything we need to enjoy.

Manna and Sabbath rest (verses 22–31)

Here Scripture speaks of a Sabbath on the seventh day.

Henry emphasizes that this day was known before the law was given at Sinai, before Israel left Egypt—indeed, from the beginning (Genesis 2:3).

Setting apart one day in seven for holy activity, together with holy rest so that the activity may be enjoyed, is, in his account, one of God's most ancient laws for humanity.

God told Israel to rest on the seventh day and ensured that this obedience would not leave them worse off.

No one ultimately loses by serving God.

They were to gather and prepare enough manna on the sixth day for two days.

This teaches us to organize our family responsibilities so that they interfere as little as possible with Sabbath worship.

Necessary tasks can still be done that day.

Nevertheless, we should seek to minimize such tasks, so that we may give ourselves more fully to preparing for the life to come.

When the Israelites kept manna against God's command, it spoiled.

When they kept it according to his command, it remained good and sweet.

Everything is made holy by God's word and prayer.

God sent no manna on the seventh day.

They were not to expect it or go out gathering it. This showed that its daily appearance was a miracle.

A portion of manna is kept as a memorial (verses 32–36)

God had fed his people with manna throughout their journey. He commanded them to preserve the memory of that mercy.

Bread already eaten should not be forgotten.

God's extraordinary works and ordinary kindnesses deserve to be remembered.

God's word is the manna by which our souls are nourished (Matthew 4:4).

The Spirit's comforts are hidden manna (Revelation 2:17).

Like the manna in the wilderness, these gifts come from heaven and sustain the spiritual life of believers on their journey through this world.

Christ, as made known in the word, must be received and applied to the soul.

The means of grace must actually be used.

Every one of us must gather for ourselves.

We should begin gathering early in life and early whenever opportunities are offered.

If we let those opportunities pass, it may become too late.

Manna was meant to be eaten, not hoarded.

Those who have received Christ must live upon him through faith rather than receive his grace without benefit.

There was enough manna for everyone, but no one had too much.

Likewise, in Christ there is enough for us all, but not more than we need.

Those who ate the manna became hungry again. They eventually died, and God was displeased with many of them.

But those who feed on Christ by faith will never hunger and will die no more.

God will be pleased with them forever.

Let us earnestly seek the Holy Spirit's grace to turn everything we know about Christ crucified into genuine spiritual nourishment through faith and love.

It is no new thing for the greatest kindness to be basely represented as the greatest injuries. They so far undervalue their deliverance, that they wished they had died in Egypt; and by the hand of the Lord, that is, by the plagues which cut off the Egyptians. We cannot suppose they had plenty in Egypt, nor could they fear dying for want in the wilderness, while they had flocks and herds: none talk more absurdly than murmurers. When we begin to fret, we ought to consider, that God hears all our murmurings. God promises a speedy and constant supply. He tried whether they would trust him, and rest satisfied with the bread of the day in its day. Thus he tried if they would serve him, and it appeared how ungrateful they were. When God plagued the Egyptians, it was to make them know he was their Lord; when he provided for the Israelites, it was to make them know he was their God.
[Exod.16.13-Exod.16.21]
Verses 13-21
At evening the quails came up, and the people caught with ease as many as they needed. The manna came down in dew. They called it "Manna, Manhu," which means, "What is this?" "It is a portion; it is that which our God has allotted us, and we will take it, and be thankful." It was pleasant food; it was wholesome food. The manna was rained from heaven; it appeared, when the dew was gone, as a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost, like coriander seed, in colour like pearls. The manna fell only six days in the week, and in double quantity on the sixth day; it bred worms and became offensive if kept more than one day, excepting on the sabbath. The people had never seen it before. It could be ground in a mill, or beaten in a mortar, and was then made into cakes and baked. It continued the forty years the Israelites were in the wilderness, wherever they went, and ceased when they arrived in Canaan. All this shows how different it was from any thing found before, or found now. They were to gather the manna every morning. We are hereby taught, 1. To be prudent and diligent in providing food for ourselves and our households; with quietness working, and eating our own bread, not the bread of idleness or deceit. God's bounty leaves room for man's duty; it did so even when manna was rained; they must not eat till they have gathered. 2. To be content with enough. Those that have most, have for themselves but food and raiment; those that have least, generally have these; so that he who gathers much has nothing over, and he who gathers little has no lack. There is not such a disproportion between one and another in the enjoyment of the things of this life, as in the mere possession of them. 3. To depend upon Providence: let them sleep quietly, though they have no bread in their tents, nor in all their camp, trusting that God, with the following day, would bring them in their daily bread. It was surer and safer in God's storehouse than their own, and would come thence sweeter and fresher. See here the folly of hoarding. The manna laid up by some, who thought themselves wiser, and better managers, than their neighbours, and who would provide lest it should fail next day, bred worms, and became good for nothing. That will prove to be most wasted, which is covetously and distrustfully spared. Such riches are corrupted, [Jas.5.2] Jas 5:2, [Jas.5.3] 3. The same wisdom, power, and goodness that brought food daily from above for the Israelites in the wilderness, brings food yearly out of the earth in the constant course of nature, and gives us all things richly to enjoy.
[Exod.16.22-Exod.16.31]

Here is mention of a seventh-day sabbath. It was known, not only before the giving of the law upon mount Sinai, but before the bringing of Israel out of Egypt, even from the beginning, [Gen.2.3] Ge 2:3. The setting apart one day in seven for holy work, and, in order to that, for holy rest, was ever since God created man upon the earth, and is the most ancient of the Divine laws. God speaks to human beings in many ways: through conscience, through the events of his providence, and through his word.

It forbids every kind of superstition and every attempt to replace God's appointed worship with inventions of our own.

Nor do they ever cease repenting.

The Lord gives further instructions about worship (verses 22–26)

Moses entered the thick darkness and heard God speak the commands that follow through the end of chapter 23.

Most of these instructions explain and apply the Ten Commandments.

The laws immediately given here concern God's worship.

God assured Israel that he would graciously receive its offerings.

Under the gospel, people are encouraged to pray everywhere.

Wherever God's people gather in his name to worship him, he is present among them.

Verses 1-2
God speaks many ways to the children of men; by conscience, by providences, by his voice, to all which we ought carefully to attend; but he never spake at any time so as he spake the TEN COMMANDMENTS. This law God had given to man before; it was written in his heart; but sin so defaced it, that it was necessary to revive the knowledge of it. The law is spiritual, and takes knowledge of the secret thoughts, desires, and dispositions of the heart. Its grand demand is love, without which outward obedience is mere hypocrisy. It requires perfect, unfailing, constant obedience; no law in the world admits disobedience to itself. Whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all, [Jas.2.10] Jas 2:10. Whether in the heart or the conduct, in thought, word, or deed, to omit or to vary any thing, is sin, and the wages of sin is death.
[Exod.20.3-Exod.20.11]
Verses 3-11
The first four of the ten commandments, commonly called the FIRST table, tell our duty to God. It was fit that those should be put first, because man had a Maker to love, before he had a neighbour to love. It cannot be expected that he should be true to his brother, who is false to his God. The first commandment concerns the object of worship, JEHOVAH, and him only. The worship of creatures is here forbidden. Whatever comes short of perfect love, gratitude, reverence, or worship, breaks this commandment. Whatsoever ye do, do all the glory of God. The second commandment refers to the worship we are to render to the Lord our God. It is forbidden to make any image or picture of the Deity, in any form, or for any purpose; or to worship any creature, image, or picture. But the spiritual import of this command extends much further. All kinds of superstition are here forbidden, and the using of mere human inventions in the worship of God. The third commandment concerns the manner of worship, that it be with all possible reverence and seriousness. All false oaths are forbidden. All light appealing to God, all profane cursing, is a horrid breach of this command. It matters not whether the word of God, or sacred things, all such-like things break this commandment, and there is no profit, honour, or pleasure in them. The Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain. The form of the fourth commandment, "Remember," shows that it was not now first given, but was known by the people before. One day in seven is to be kept holy. Six days are allotted to worldly business, but not so as to neglect the service of God, and the care of our souls. On those days we must do all our work, and leave none to be done on the sabbath day. Christ allowed works of necessity, charity, and piety; for the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath, [Mark.2.27] Mr 2:27; but all works of luxury, vanity, or self-indulgence in any form, are forbidden. Trading, paying wages, settling accounts, writing letters of business, worldly studies, trifling visits, journeys, or light conversation, are not keeping this day holy to the Lord. Sloth and indolence may be a carnal, but not a holy rest. The sabbath of the Lord should be a day of rest from worldly labour, and a rest in the service of God. The advantages from the due keeping of this holy day, were it only to the health and happiness of mankind, with the time it affords for taking care of the soul, show the excellency of this commandment. The day is blessed; men are blessed by it, and in it. The blessing and direction to keep holy are not limited to the seventh day, but are spoken of the sabbath day.
[Exod.20.12-Exod.20.17]
Verses 12-17
The laws of the SECOND table, that is, the last six of the ten commandments, state our duty to ourselves and to one another, and explain the great commandment, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, [Luke.10.27] Lu 10:27. Godliness and honesty must go together. The fifth commandment concerns the duties we owe to our relations. Honour thy father and thy mother, includes esteem of them, shown in our conduct; obedience to their lawful commands; come when they call you, go where they send you, do what they bid you, refrain from what they forbid you; and this, as children, cheerfully, and from a principle of love. Also submission to their counsels and corrections. Endeavouring, in every thing, to comfort parents, and to make their old age easy; maintaining them if they need support, which our Saviour makes to be particularly intended in this commandment, [Matt.15.4-Matt.15.6] Mt 15:4-6. Careful observers have noted a peculiar blessing in temporal things on obedient, and the reverse on disobedient children. The sixth commandment requires that we regard the life and the safety of others as we do our own. Magistrates and their officers, and witnesses testifying the truth, do not break this command. Self-defence is lawful; but much which is not deemed murder by the laws of man, is such before God. Furious passions, stirred up by anger or by drunkenness, are no excuse: more guilty is murder in duels, which is a horrible effect of a haughty, revengeful spirit. All fighting, whether for wages, for renown, or out of anger and malice, breaks this command, and the bloodshed therein is murder. To tempt men to vice and crimes which shorten life, may be included. Misconduct, such as may break the heart, or shorten the lives of parents, wives, or other relatives, is a breach of this command. This command forbids all envy, malice, hatred, or anger, all provoking or insulting language. The destruction of our own lives is here forbidden. This commandment requires a spirit of kindness, longsuffering, and forgiveness. The seventh commandment concerns chastity. We should be as much afraid of that which defiles the body, as of that which destroys it. Whatever tends to pollute the imagination, or to raise the passions, falls under this law, as impure pictures, books, conversation, or any other like matters. The eighth commandment is the law of love as it respects the property of others. The portion of worldly things allotted us, as far as it is obtained in an honest way, is the bread which God hath given us; for that we ought to be thankful, to be contented with it, and, in the use of lawful means, to trust Providence for the future. Imposing upon the ignorance, easiness, or necessity of others, and many other things, break God's law, though scarcely blamed in society. Plunderers of kingdoms though above human justice, will be included in this sentence. Defrauding the public, contracting debts without prospect of paying them, or evading payment of just debts, extravagance, all living upon charity when not needful, all squeezing the poor in their wages; these, and such things, break this command; which requires industry, frugality, and content, and to do to others, about worldly property, as we would they should do to us. The ninth commandment concerns our own and our neighbour's good name. This forbids speaking falsely on any matter, lying, equivocating, and any way devising or designing to deceive our neighbour. Speaking unjustly against our neighbour, to hurt his reputation. Bearing false witness against him, or in common conversation slandering, backbiting, and tale-bearing; making what is done amiss, worse than it is, and in any way endeavouring to raise our reputation upon the ruin of our neighbour's. How much this command is every day broken among persons of all ranks! The tenth commandment strikes at the root; Thou shalt not covet. The others forbid all desire of doing what will be an injury to our neighbour; this forbids all wrong desire of having what will gratify ourselves.
[Exod.20.18-Exod.20.21]
Verses 18-21
This law, which is so extensive that we cannot measure it, so spiritual that we cannot evade it, and so reasonable that we cannot find fault with it, will be the rule of the future judgment of God, as it is for the present conduct of man. If tried by this rule, we shall find our lives have been passed in transgressions. And with this holy law and an awful judgment before us, who can despise the gospel of Christ? And the knowledge of the law shows our need of repentance. In every believer's heart sin is dethroned and crucified, the law of God is written, and the image of God renewed. The Holy Spirit enables him to hate sin and flee from it, to love and keep this law in sincerity and truth; nor will he cease to repent.
[Exod.20.22-Exod.20.26]
Verses 22-26
Moses having entered into the thick darkness, God there spake in his hearing all that follows from hence to the end of chap. 23, which is mostly an exposition of the ten commandments. The laws in these verses relate to God's worship. The Israelites are assured of God's gracious acceptance of their devotions. Under the gospel, men are encouraged to pray every where, and wherever God's people meet in his name to worship him, he will be in the midst of them; there he will come unto them, and will bless them.
